meeting_header: Recorded: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC · Duration: 48m · Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Brooks (Redwood SE), Oliver Grant (Stormfront Head of ML), Priya Rao (Infra Lead), Daniel Kim (CTO)
summary: Discovery focused on cost/unit economics for model inference. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments; primary concerns are per-token costs, latency SLOs for trader-facing assistants, batching and KV/prefix caching opportunities, and budget constraints for pilot. Agreed next steps: send pricing matrix, run dedicated throughput benchmark, customer to share workload traces.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, how are we doing?
[00:05] Oliver: doing good, thanks, excited to dig in — we mainly want to understand cost per model call across different deployment modes.
[00:12] Maya: perfect, we'll focus on unit economics and the levers you can pull — Ethan will cover the technical stuff.
[00:18] Ethan: hi all, quick note my mic is a bit windy so sorry for background noise.
[00:25] Daniel: no worries. so Oliver, remind us of the workload — is this trader assistant inference at low latency, or batch scoring?
[00:33] Oliver: mostly near-real-time chat for desk traders, sub-200ms for the 95th percentile is ideal, but we can tolerate up to 400ms for heavier ops. throughput is moderate — about 150 qps peak, but spikes to 400 during market open. token lengths average 120 tokens per request, sometimes 600 for research summaries.
[00:54] Priya: and for context — our annual budget for this pilot is strictly capped, we'd like to estimate monthly run-rate if this goes to prod. so cost-per-1M-tokens type numbers are what the execs ask for.
[01:10] Maya: got it. for hosted APIs we usually quote per-1k or per-1M token tiers — but the big levers are batching, caching, and quantization. quick example numbers ballpark: hosted can be about $X per 1M tokens for gen models at baseline, whereas dedicated reserved capacity brings the marginal per-token to a lower effective price because of fixed monthly commit — i can send a sheet with concrete brackets.
[01:32] Oliver: can you give a concrete example? like if we run 100M tokens a month what are we talking about on hosted vs dedicated?
[01:38] Ethan: sure — rough simplified math: hosted is pay-as-you-go so assume higher per-token rate but no infra commit; dedicated you pay a monthly reserved node pool which amortizes GPU costs. so for 100M tokens hosted might be, say, Y to Z, while dedicated with a medium commit could shave 30–50% off unit cost — depends on utilization, sequence lengths, and batching.
[01:58] Priya: the devil's in the details — how much does batching actually help given low latency requirements?
[02:04] Ethan: great question. batching increases GPU throughput by combining multiple requests into a single kernel execution — it's very effective for throughput and lowers per-token GPU time. but it adds latency; with smart continuous-batching we can keep added latency to 10–30ms when queueing short windows. for trader use-cases where strict <200ms P95 is needed, we tune batch sizes and use latency-first routing. you still get some efficiency gains, but not as much as high-latency batch workloads.
[02:30] Oliver: what about caching? we have a lot of repetitive prefixes — trade instruction templates, static context, etc.
[02:36] Ethan: KV/prefix caching is a big win there — if 40% of tokens are repeat prefixes, effective tokens billed drop proportionally for those calls. Redwood supports automatic prefix/KV caching and we can measure hit rates during the benchmark. that can be as impactful as batching in some workflows.
[02:55] Daniel: curious about quantization — any noticeable quality loss for our domain-specific prompts?
[02:59] Ethan: quantization (8-bit/4-bit) is model dependent; many open models maintain high quality on 8-bit and some 4-bit workflows are acceptable. the tradeoff is lower memory and higher throughput. we'd recommend a quick eval with your prompts; during the pilot we can run quality regressions tied to your prompt set.
[03:17] Priya: security: if we go dedicated or private we need VPC peering and KMS integration — any limitations?
[03:24] Maya: we support VPC/private control plane options, customer-managed KMS, and audit logs. for SOC2/ISO we have docs — i'll include the pack. dedicated can be single-tenant GPU pools with stricter network isolation.
[03:36] Oliver: perfect. back to numbers — do you have a worked example that includes cache hit rate and batching assumptions? execs want scenarios (pessimistic/likely/optimistic).
[03:45] Maya: yes — we typically show three scenarios: low-efficiency (no cache, minimal batching), medium (30–50% cache hit, small continuous batching), high-efficiency (60%+ cache, aggressive batching for non-latency paths). i'll send an itemized sheet with per-1M-token math and assumed latency buckets.
[03:58] Ethan: for benchmarks we'll need representative traces — token size distribution, inter-arrival times. Priya, can you share a sample of anonymized traces?
[04:06] Priya: yes, we'll scrub PII and provide traces. aim for what window? 48 hours?
[04:10] Ethan: 48 is good to capture market open/close spikes. we'll run both hosted tests and a dedicated reserved config to show differential.
[04:18] Oliver: what about cold-start and KV cache warm-up? that skews early numbers.
[04:22] Ethan: right — warm-up matters. we'll run a warm-up phase and report steady-state and first-hour metrics. caching hit rates will increase over the first few hours as KV is populated.
[04:31] Daniel: do you support fallback routing? like if dedicated pool maxes out we still want graceful degradation to hosted with higher latency but availability preserved.
[04:38] Maya: yes, smart routing with fallback policies is supported — can route by latency, cost, or region. that is part of recommended production setup to avoid outages during spikes.
[04:46] Oliver: can we get an estimate for egress and networking costs in private deployments? that's a big unknown for our infra team.
[04:52] Priya: yes network egress can be material.
[04:55] Ethan: for private on-prem it's customer network egress; for VPC connections we quantify cross-region transfers. we'll add a placeholder estimate and we can work with your infra team to refine.
[05:03] Maya: quick commercial note — hosted is fast to start and gets you immediate usage data; dedicated is best when you need predictable latency and cost for sustained load; private is primarily for regulatory/air-gapped needs. many customers start hosted for discovery then shift to dedicated when they hit a commit threshold.
[05:18] Oliver: what threshold? like what monthly tokens typically trigger dedicated interest?
[05:22] Ethan: generally once steady-state consumption is large enough that reserved capacity amortization is beneficial — often above a few tens of millions of tokens/month depending on model. that's why our pricing matrix shows breakpoints.
[05:33] Priya: do you offer burst capacity? market opens are spiky and we don't want dropped requests.
[05:37] Maya: yes dedicated has burst options and auto-scaling policies; you can configure guaranteed baseline and a burst bucket for short spikes.
[05:44] Daniel: how do you measure unit cost — are you exposing per-token GPU utilization and cost breakdown?
[05:49] Ethan: Redwood Console shows token-level cost, GPU time breakdown, batching efficiency, and per-route dashboards. we'll include sample screenshots in the deck.
[05:58] Oliver: ok, sample scenario then — using our trace with average 120 tokens, 150 qps baseline, 400 qps spikes, with 40% repeat prefixes and target P95 <200ms. what do you estimate for monthly spend at 30M tokens?
[06:12] Maya: i'll model three scenarios but very roughly: hosted might be the highest, dedicated mid, and if you get good cache hit/dedic amz it could be 30–45% cheaper than hosted. exact numbers in sheet.
[06:22] Priya: we need the math live — can you walk through a sample per-1M token calc now?
[06:26] Ethan: sure — assume baseline model cost is A per 1M tokens (compute + infra). with 40% cache hit effective billable tokens drop to 0.6M for that same work. batching that keeps latency constraints might yield another 10–20% effective improvement. so multiply factors: A * 0.6 * 0.85 ~ 0.51A effective — about half the naive cost.
[06:47] Oliver: that's great to see. any hidden fees we should expect? like storage for KV cache or log retention extra charges?
[06:53] Maya: some add-ons like extended observability retention or premium SLAs are add-ons. KV cache is part of the platform; storage for long-term embeddings or heavy audit retention may incur charges — we'll detail those.
[07:03] Daniel: do you support bringing-your-own-model and still use Redwood runtime optimizations?
[07:08] Ethan: yes — you can bring models; our runtime does kernel selection and quantization-aware execution for many open and customer models. performance varies by architecture though.
[07:18] Priya: benchmark question: for dedicated runs do you give raw metrics (p95, p99, tokens/sec) and cost per token?
[07:24] Ethan: yes, benchmark report will include p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and estimated cost-per-million tokens under those conditions.
[07:33] Oliver: timeline — we want to decide on pilot in two weeks. can Redwood commit to a benchmark and pricing sheet in that window?
[07:38] Maya: yes — we can get the pricing sheet and kick off the benchmark within 48–72 hours after we get traces.
[07:44] Priya: sounds good. any other performance tips to reduce cost without hurting latency?
[07:49] Ethan: a few: 1) move deterministic parts of prompts to KV cache; 2) precompute embeddings for static content; 3) use smaller model variants for non-critical paths; 4) tune batching windows dynamically per route.
[08:01] Daniel: competitor question — we evaluate Anthropic and OpenAI as well; how does Redwood's unit economics compare?
[08:08] Maya: Redwood focuses on serving efficiency and routing — we can show relative examples but exact numbers depend on model and workload. often the advantage comes from reserved capacity plus caching and batching — you get better unit economics than vanilla hosted APIs when utilization is decent.
[08:23] Oliver: ok let's recap next steps.
[08:26] Maya: recap: (1) Priya shares anonymized workload traces (48 hours) by 2026-03-08; (2) Ethan runs hosted + dedicated benchmark starting ~2026-03-06 and posts results; (3) Maya sends pricing matrix and security pack by 2026-03-10; (4) follow-up call to review results week of 2026-03-15.
[08:49] Priya: confirmed. one small ask — include example change in unit cost if we move from 16-bit to 8-bit quantization.
[08:56] Ethan: will include quantization sensitivity in the benchmark report.
[09:00] Maya: awesome, thanks everyone. we'll share notes and links after the call.
[09:05] Oliver: thanks — appreciate the detail.
[09:08] Daniel: thanks all. bye.
[09:10] -- meeting ends --

Notes: transcription contains a few minor transcription artifacts; proper nouns may be slightly off. The numeric placeholders (A, X, Y, Z) will be replaced by concrete figures in the pricing sheet Maya will send.
